item.description:
Asobi 0.2 (build 537)

  • Web shares are a quarter of the size, and they stream. The review proxy was being encoded at about 26 Mbps for a 1080p clip — 232 MB for a minute of picture, several times what Frame.io or Vimeo send, and more than a normal connection can keep up with. It now encodes in the same band those services use: 5.7 Mbps, 65 MB for that same minute, measured at 0.991 structural similarity to the old encode across the busiest part of the shot. If a job needs the old weight, webshare.bitrateFactor still sets it.
  • The web page buffers like a player instead of a straw. It used to pull three to five seconds of video, one segment at a time, waiting for each. It now pulls twenty seconds at once and quietly caches the whole clip behind the review, so a clip you have watched once plays like a local file.
  • The web review's controls fit a scaled window. On a 14" screen with the window not full — which is what a call looks like — the transport and the markup tools ran off both ends of the bar. The bar wraps now, transport on one row and markup on the next, with nothing off-screen at any width.
  • The web playlist is findable. It was behind an unlabelled button and the letter G. The line in the header that says which clip you're on now opens it.
  • Fixed: a reviewer who can't export could reach Share to Web. Moving it out of a sheet and into the Shared Review panel moved it past the menu's role gating. It follows the same rule as the exports again.

Asobi 0.2 (build 534)

  • Sharing a review to the web happens in one window. Session ▸ Shared Review… now holds the whole thing: the passcode for anyone joining from Asobi, and under it the web link — the two choices, the button, the link itself, and End Review. The separate Share to Web sheet is gone, and Session ▸ Share to Web… opens the same window rather than a second one on top of it.
  • Start Web Share works from a standing start. With nothing running, one click hosts the session and publishes the link. The passcode above the button is what people joining from Asobi use, so the session turning up alongside the link isn't a surprise.
  • You can see how far a share has got. A progress bar runs across the whole playlist while it encodes and uploads, with the clip it's working on named underneath — rather than a line of text that changes every few minutes.
  • Web shares are about five times faster. Making one used to seek to every frame of the movie individually: a 730-frame 1080p clip spent 12.5 of its 15.5 seconds doing nothing but decoding. It reads the movie straight through now — the same clip takes 3.3 seconds. Rendered image sequences are unchanged; they never paid that cost.
  • A finished share stops offering to start itself again. Pressing Start Web Share after a long encode used to run the whole thing a second time — and quietly kill the link, since a new share means a new link and anyone watching the old one loses the review. Once a share exists, the button is replaced by the link and End Review, and re-encoding is a separate choice that says what it costs before it does anything.
  • Files you drop add to the playlist instead of replacing it. Dropping a movie or a sequence folder onto the picture used to throw away the review you had open. Drops append now, in the order you dropped them, and the playhead stays where it is. Dropping into an empty window still loads and plays what you dropped, and session files, invites and folders of shots behave exactly as before.
  • Fixed: an optimized bundle made from QuickTimes explained nothing. Optimized stand-ins are encoded from rendered image sequences, so a session of movie files produced "0 shots" and a folder of full-size copies with no word about why. The save dialog now says so before you pick a location, and the finishing message tells you what actually traveled — how many shots were optimized, and how many went as they are.
  • Fixed: three View menu items looked like their icons had gone missing. Layout Grid, Notes Sidebar and Keyboard Shortcuts sat indented against an empty column, because macOS was aligning them to the Enter Full Screen icon that the system adds to that menu. They sit flush again.

Asobi 0.2 (build 523)

  • Export a side-by-side comparison as a QuickTime. File ▸ Export ▸ Export Movie with Burn-ins ▸ Side-by-Side Movie… writes the A/B compare as one movie — left/right or top/bottom — with each side at its own full resolution rather than the squeezed halves the on-screen mode uses. Each side keeps its own grade, look stack and input color space, carries its own marks, and gets a name plate and its own frame number, so a note about "the B side at 1043" can't be misread. The compare's sync offset carries over, and a shorter B holds its last frame instead of cutting to black.
  • A size control, because 4K against 4K is 8192 pixels across. That's an enormous file and past what H.264 will even encode. Pick 100 / 75 / 50 / 33 / 25 % of the A frame per side and the dialog shows the resulting output dimensions before you commit. The frame is exactly the two halves — a 1920×1080 pair exports 1920×540 across or 960×1080 stacked, never padded out to 16:9 — and a side of a different shape letterboxes inside its own half rather than being stretched.
  • Whole sessions export the same way. Set Export to "Whole session" and it walks every A/B pair — the ones you marked with the A/B chips on the playlist rows, or, with nothing marked, the first two rows of each version group — into one continuous movie. Every shot against its previous version, in a single file.
  • Asobi now reads a file's color instead of assuming it. Color ▸ Check This File's Color… (or click the color chip) opens a wizard that reads the file, shows you the same frame decoded every plausible way side by side, and asks what screen you're on. A lot of what it reports isn't a guess: an EXR's header states its primaries, a QuickTime usually carries the encoder's own color tags, anything brighter than 1.0 has to be scene-linear, and a black floor sitting around 0.09 with no highlights is a log curve. Pick the one that looks right — you don't have to know what ACEScg means to see which of six pictures is correct.
  • The color chip warns you when a file disagrees with how it's being shown. It turns amber and says what it thinks the file actually is. It won't interrupt a review with a dialog, it stays quiet on clips you've already given a color space, and it says nothing when the file genuinely doesn't state one. Settings turns the checking off.
  • The side-by-side export comes out the way round you're looking at it. In Side by Side (Top/Bottom) on screen, the movie is top/bottom; in left/right, so is the movie. The dialog still lets you override it.
  • Fixed: rendered sequences were being treated as still images. "Apply to all" filed a sequence's — or a movie's — color space under the one stills use, then applied it to every still and QuickTime in the playlist alongside the clips you meant. Sequences, movies and stills are told apart properly now, and the wording says which ("every EXR sequence", "every movie"). What you saw on screen was never affected; this was the bulk operation and the remembered per-format default.
  • Fixed: the whole Compare menu was dead. Wipe, Difference, both Side by Side modes, Stack, Clear Compare and ⌘\ Flip were all greyed out for the entire life of a compare — the menu never noticed a B side had been loaded. Everything in that menu works again.
